author: ticktockbent
body:
Add `soph omega publish` and `soph omega status --verify` so an approved three-root manifest can be published and checked through the actual HTTPS trust client. A successful local write alone no longer counts as successful publication.

The first backend writes a dedicated local directory served by separately configured HTTPS. Explicit consecutive release versions identify approvals: retrying the same version/manifest reuses the exact recorded signatures and expiry; changing membership or repairing expired approval requires the next version. The publisher keeps an immutable, linked release journal beside the authority, takes network and destination locks, installs immutable objects before atomically replacing `timestamp.json`, and refuses conflicting objects or publication state missing from the journal. The committed authority stays unchanged.

Verification uses a fresh durable bootstrap client and compares the accepted versions, root manifest, and hashes of the exact authenticated metadata against the prepared release. It also fetches the initial numbered root. Status exposes role deadlines, roots, and historical verification/failure receipts; offline status does not claim current availability. The operator guide documents the command surface, ordering, retry, retention, and recovery boundaries.

This remains Linux/disposable-only. Unattended renewal with separate online keys, rotation, production custody/hosting, the release-gate migration, and discovery-consumer adoption remain subsequent slices. Schema 1 authority custody remains permanently disposable-only. The `/omega/` hosting/base-path plan and Vercel configuration are unchanged; no production keys or network are deployed.

Validation:

- `make build` and the repository race suite.
- Disposable-key HTTPS tests: first publication, identical retry, membership update and returning-client rollback rejection; staged/timestamp interruptions; process-kill recovery; torn writes; conflicting immutable files; missing/corrupt history; expiry requiring a higher repair; concurrent publishers and lock cancellation.
- Verification rejects outage/stale responses, missing objects, wrong signatures, valid same-version metadata with different bytes, redirects, TLS bypass, and unsafe filesystem paths.
- CLI integration tests and a smoke run of the built binary with a temporary HTTPS server and trusted rehearsal CA: init, publish, identical retry, and `status --verify`.
- Windows CLI cross-compilation, local documentation links, and `git diff --check`.

Relates to #195, #197, and #199; these remain open for the rest of the lifecycle and legacy-tool retirement.

author: jefedavis
body:
## Description

The post-delete Helm hook creates a cleanup `DaemonSet` and a naked cleanup-wait `Pod`. The `DaemonSet` correctly passes through `imagePullSecrets`, `tolerations`, and `podSecurityContext` from `values.yaml`, but the naked `Pod` did not inherit any of them. On clusters that require image pull secrets, node tolerations, or that enforce Pod Security Standards, this prevented the hook Pod from scheduling or running.

This change applies `imagePullSecrets`, `tolerations`, `podSecurityContext`, and the container `securityContext` to the cleanup-wait `Pod`, and also adds the missing container `securityContext` to the cleanup `DaemonSet` container for consistency. No new values are introduced; all four already exist and are used by the DaemonSet.

## Testing

`helm lint` passes and `helm template` renders all four fields correctly on both the DaemonSet and the naked Pod when the values are set.

Fixes #1536

## AI disclosure

Per the project [AI Policy](https://github.com/spegel-org/spegel/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md): this change was drafted by me and prepared with assistance from an LLM (Claude Opus 4.8 via Claude Code). The LLM was used to help validate rendering with `helm lint`/`helm template`; I reviewed and take responsibility for the change.

author: kudoscards
body:
Phases **C3** and **C5** of `docs/click-and-forget-plan.md`, in two commits. Between them, click and forget is complete.

> **Why both are here.** C3 was opened alone and went green on `0771d2e`; I pushed C5 to the same branch before merging it, which added it to this PR. That was my mistake. Rewriting the branch to split them would invalidate the green run and gain nothing, so the PR now describes both — the two commits are cleanly separated and can be reviewed one at a time.

---

# C3 — Letting the catalog describe itself (ADR 0259)

A `CardDesign` carried a category, a name, a slug, a SKU and a thumbnail, and nothing that said **who it suits**. So "select one of those cards based on the receiver's profile" had nothing to read, and #486 shipped automatic approval picking by hash, saying plainly it was a placeholder.

Vocabulary chosen by the user: `any / child / teen / adult` and `funny / warm / elegant / simple`.

**Authored in Airtable, not an ops screen.** The catalog already lives there (ADR 0011), the re-export pass is happening there anyway, and the sync's field matching is already tolerant — `Age Band` also answers to `Age`, `Age Group`, `Suits`, `Audience`. Being the **only** author is what makes a cleared cell correctly clear the column rather than lose data.

**Null is deliberately not `any`.** Null means nobody has described this design; `any` means somebody looked and said it suits everybody. A selection rule has to tell silence from a claim — and it is why the column has no default, which would have asserted on behalf of 217 unexamined designs that each suits a four-year-old and a retiree equally.

**Age degrades safely, which is the point.** A recipient's age is unknowable whenever `birthYearKnown` is false — every CleanCloud contact by design (ADR 0252) — so the common case is unknown age against an undescribed or `any` card, and that case had to be the safe one.

**An unplaceable word is reported, not swallowed.** "Middle-aged" stores null exactly like an empty cell; the only difference is whether anyone finds out. Each sync now carries `attributes.undescribed / total` (the ops pass's progress bar) and `attributes.unknownValues` (named with the card it was on).

Runbook: `docs/ops/catalog-describe-designs.md`.

---

# C5 — Where a chosen message goes (ADR 0260)

The message pool had been saved and unread since #485. This prints it, and settles the question that ADR deliberately left open.

**Settled with evidence.** The editor updates elements by id (`design-editor-client.tsx:512`), so the seeded `inside-message` block survives every text edit and dies only when somebody deletes it and types a fresh one — exactly when it stops being trustworthy. So: that block if present, else the only text block on the inside page, else **nothing**, because two candidates is a design somebody built deliberately and choosing between them is a coin toss printed on a card that cannot be recalled.

**The e2e caught a real mistake in the first version.** I refused to add a block at all — two messages stacked on one face is a defect this codebase already has machinery for after it shipped twice. But that meant a design with *no* inside text got no message, and that is not rare: a member's own uploaded artwork starts blank (ADR 0026), and so does a catalog card with no Airtable inside message. So the rule is narrower than "never add": **never add beside existing text**. An empty page has nothing to stack against, and the block written there uses the builder's own geometry, pinned by a test.

**A card with no readable slot still goes**, carrying the design's own words — a birthday with no card is the larger failure. The dashboard **names** those cards rather than counting them, and asks by *running the real placement* over the design rather than reimplementing it: a second copy of "where does a message go" would drift from the one that prints.

**Chosen at approval, applied at send**, so it can be seen before printing and a pool edited tomorrow cannot rewrite a card going out today. Its FK is `SET NULL` where the design's is `RESTRICT` — rewriting a pool is ordinary and must not be blocked; a missing design is a card with no artwork.

**The design pick now reads C3's columns.** Undescribed beats a mismatched band (silence is a smaller risk than a card marked for someone else's age), and it prefers without ever excluding, so a nursery whose whole pool is children's cards still sends to the contact whose age we were never told. The message pick is salted differently, or four designs and four messages would only ever produce four of sixteen pairings.

---

## Verification

Lint, typecheck, **1,371 API + 317 web unit tests**, **all 885 e2e tests** and the full build, green locally. `prisma migrate diff` confirms both migrations match the schema exactly.

**Twelve mutations across the two commits, all caught.** The C3 pair worth noting *correctly survived* the e2e — which mocks the catalog source and so never runs the parser — and were caught by the vocabulary unit spec. The C5 six covered every way the placement could print the wrong thing: choosing when ambiguous, ignoring the seeded id, appending instead of replacing, writing beside existing text, mutating the caller's document, and counting non-text elements as candidates.

**Two test fixtures were lying, and one passed by luck.** Both saved designs in the age-band tests pointed at the same catalog row, so the second `describeDesign` silently overwrote the first. Fixed so each has its own template.

## Notes

- Two additive migrations. C3: two nullable columns, two Postgres enums, a partial index. C5: one nullable FK column and a partial index. No rows rewritten by either.
- A fourth repo guard fired: `card-artwork-single-source` made me declare why `standing-orders.service.ts` now reads a design document (to ask whether a message would land, by running the real placement — it never copies or changes it).
- **Not built, deliberately:** drafting messages with a model. `source: "assisted"` is recorded and nothing writes it. That is a vendor and a data-processing agreement, and the pool it would write into now demonstrably works.
- `docs/backlog.md` records the `engine-resilience` intermittent test I hit twice during verification — passes in 2.3s alone, never failed CI. The fix is an explicit timeout matching what it does, not skipping it, and I did not widen these PRs to do it.

Recorded as ADR 0259 and ADR 0260.

author: jkitchin
body:
Two bugs found while writing the ODE chapters of the book.

## 1. A profile of a combination on an ODE model came back flat

```python
profile_likelihood(exp, data, "k2")                 # bounded [0.189, 0.207]
profile_likelihood(exp, data, expression="k2")      # shape='flat', ci=(None, None)
```

`DevianceFunction` read the measurement error from a `measurement_error`
attribute. An `ODEExperiment` does not have one — it keeps `sigma`, keyed by
the measured state behind a `state@time` response name — so `getattr(...,
1.0)` silently used σ = 1. With a true σ of 0.01 the deviance is 10,000× too
small, so it never crosses the χ² threshold and every profile looks flat.

- All the spellings are resolved now (`measurement_error` mapping or scalar,
  `sigma` keyed by the state behind `state@time`).
- An experiment that reports no measurement error **warns** rather than
  quietly assuming 1, since the deviance scale decides every interval.
- The predict path now takes its gradient from the experiment's own
  sensitivity matrix where it has one, instead of finite differences: the
  case above went from 2.25 s to 0.26 s.

Both forms now agree to six digits.

## 2. Every new parameter value retraced the FIM Jacobian

The compiled Jacobian was cached per set of nominal parameter values, so
anything that moves the parameters — a robust design over draws, a profile, a
Monte Carlo over the posterior — paid a full trace per draw (0.15 s against
0.0002 s cached; a robust-design build in the book cost 400–750 s).

The Jacobian maps `x*`, which *carries* the parameter values, so it does not
depend on the nominals; only the model could, since `create_model` receives
them. A kernel is now reused whenever the model the new values build is
structurally identical: variables, bounds, response expressions, measurement
errors, and the identity of the callables behind any custom node — which a
`repr` cannot see, and which is decisive because any dependence on the
nominals has to be created inside `create_model`, making a fresh object.

Still recompiles, with tests for each: a model that folds a nominal value into
its response expression, one that hides it in a custom node, and an experiment
edited after a first call (reuse requires a matching fingerprint, which caught
a real hole in the first version of this change).

New θ dropped from 0.15 s to 0.0003 s, and 25 random draws give bitwise the
same FIM as a cache-cleared rebuild.

## Tests

805 passed, 1 skipped (`-m "slow or not slow"`), ruff clean. Four new tests:
the deviance matches the estimator's objective and its analytic gradient
matches finite differences; `expression="k2"` matches `parameter_name="k2"`;
a parameter sweep reuses the kernel and still equals the uncached autodiff

author: blackpi3
body:
`category` is the field that answers questions about a *kind* of thing rather than one product. All five existing insights group by `product_id`, so none of them can say how much I spend on chips, or how often I buy milk.

The field could not answer either, because it was free text:

- **79 of 181** products had no category at all
- **two vocabularies mixed** — hand-written `Dairy`, `Snacks`, `Personal Care` alongside Open Food Facts taxonomy leaves `cut`, `chia`, `stuffed wafers`, `cooked chicken breast slices`
- **inconsistent depth** — `Cleaning` next to `Cleaning / Dishwashing`, `Produce` next to `Produce / Vegetables`

**46 distinct values over 181 products.** Six bags of crisps sat under `Snacks`, `flavoured potato crisps`, `corn chips` and two nulls.

## What this adds

A closed vocabulary in code: **13 branches → 32 sections → 111 categories**.

```
Molkereiprodukte & Eier  ->  Käse  ->  Reibekäse
branch                       section   category
```

Three levels because the shopper wants to zoom: ~10 readable bars for "where the money goes", the fine level underneath for "how often do I buy chips".

## Decisions worth reviewing

**The leaf is stored; section and branch are derived.** A product will carry only `reibekaese`. This is the lesson `is_budget_brand` cost us — the same fact copied onto 181 rows drifts, and extending a table does not reach rows already written. Regrouping is now a one-line edit to `SECTIONS`, and two products cannot disagree about which branch `chips` is in, because neither carries the answer.

**Lifted from the shops, not invented.** ALDI SÜD publishes a 153-leaf tree over its whole store; GLOBUS a three-level one whose third level is in the product URLs the crawl never recorded. Both are German, human-designed, already at shopping-list granularity — and they beat a keyword reading exactly where it fails. GLOBUS files Kaffeesahne under `kaffeesahne-kondensmilch`; matching on "Kaffee" files a cream under coffee.

**But the shops are not the contract.** They disagree about shape — `Käse` is top-level at ALDI and nested under dairy at GLOBUS — and ALDI's tree mixes in `Garten`, `Kleidung` and marketing tags like `Markenprodukte` and `XXL`. If the hierarchy were one shop's, the other shop's purchases could not be placed in it, and cross-store comparison is the point of the project. Their trees propose; this vocabulary decides. The same relationship the project already has with Open Food Facts.

**`Obst` / `Gemüse` / `Kräuter`, never a single `Produce`** — "Produce" cannot tell you how much fruit you bought.

**Keys ascii, labels German.** Identity is `reibekaese`, the word shown is `Reibekäse`. `produce.py` already names the coupling this avoids: there the vocabulary key doubles as the product name, which is the one thing that must be unpicked for a second market.

**A category must be recognisable, not merely true.** OFF filed a chicken breast under `cut`. That is not false — it *was* a cut — but it tells a person nothing about what is in the bag. Truth is not the bar.

## Accuracy

Matching on product name alone reaches **177 of 181**, touching all 13 branches. The retailer-derived list fixed most of what a hand-drafted one got wrong: `Salami Edelschimmel` → `salami` (a keyword match read "Schimmel" and filed it under cleaning products), `Kaffeesahne` → `sahne`, `Gouda jung` → `schnittkaese`, `Pufuleti` → `chips`.

**Seven are still wrong (~4%)**, all the same pattern — a flavour or ingredient word beating the head noun:

| product | proposed | should be |
|---|---|---|
| `Linsen Chips Paprika` | `paprika-chili` | `chips` |
| `Eis, Schokolade` | `schokolade` | `speiseeis` |
| `Eisschale Chocolate Chip` | `schokolade` | `speiseeis` |
| `Börek Stange Spinat` | `salat` | `herzhaftes-gebaeck` |
| `TUC Bread snack rolls` | `brot` | `cracker` |
| `Mozzarella, gerieben` ×2 | `weichkaese` | `reibekaese` |

No cleverer matcher was built to chase these. "Rightmost noun wins" fixes `Linsenchips` and breaks `Eis, Schokolade`. Catching them is the propose/confirm loop's job, as it is for produce and the catalogues.

Four products match nothing: `Milk (1.5% fat, ESL)`, `KitKat Tablet Hazelnut`, `Bubble Chill Wildberry`, `Blitzstart Mix`.

## Tests

20 tests on made-up tables. `problems()` takes the tables as arguments so each check is exercised on invented data, including the alias-collision check — an alias claimed by two categories makes a proposal a coin toss, and a coin toss written down is the failure this vocabulary exists to remove.

Full suite: `207 passed`, ruff clean.

## Not in this PR

Nothing reads the vocabulary yet — this is additive, no behaviour change.

- the 181 products still carry their old 46 values
- the brandless invariant in `product_store.py` still tests `category.startswith("Produce")` and needs to call `is_produce()`
- there is no `category propose` / `confirm` CLI
- `insights.py` still does not group by any of it

A `u0` of eltype `Float32` reached PETSc's double build and failed with `No matching function wrapper was found!` from inside FunctionWrappers, which says nothing about the cause. It now raises an `ArgumentError` naming the eltype and what to do: `remake(prob; u0 = Float64.(prob.u0))`. A `DAEProblem`'s `du0` is checked the same way. Complex and BigFloat states were already refused, by SciMLBase, before reaching here.

Whole numbers still work, converted as OrdinaryDiffEq converts them: `[1]` solves and returns Float64. PETSc does ship single precision and complex builds, and using them is a larger change than this; the message says only what this package supports today.

author: christian-heusel
body:
### Description

`PUT /api/v1/secrets/{namespace}/{name}` reads the secret, modifies it and then calls `Update`. If the secret is changed by someone else between the read and the write, the Kubernetes API rejects the `Update` with a `Conflict` error because the `resourceVersion` is stale. The handler had no branch for that error, so it fell through to `serverErrorResponse` and returned `500 Internal Server Error`.

The OpenAPI spec already declares `409 Conflict` for this endpoint, and the other write handlers (delete secret, delete PVC, delete workspace, delete WorkspaceKind) already map `apierrors.IsConflict` to `conflictResponse`. With a 500, clients can't tell a retryable concurrent-modification error from a real server failure.

### Changes

- `api/secrets_handler.go`: in `UpdateSecretHandler`, add an `apierrors.IsConflict(err)` branch that returns `conflictResponse` with the status causes, matching the existing handlers.

The repository (`SecretRepository.UpdateSecret`) already returns the Kubernetes error from `client.Update` unwrapped, so no repository change is needed. The swagger annotations already list 409, so `openapi/` is unchanged.

author: benjamindemaille
body:
### What's wrong

`CmdlineAllocString()` malloc()s exactly `strlen + 1` bytes, but some consumers walk the copy with `Strchrnul()`. On non-glibc platforms that is `rawmemchr2()`, which reads a whole vector at a time and can run up to `kBytesPerVec - 1` bytes past the terminator. `ParseAttribCondition()` does this on the `--attrib` / `--attrib-indiv` condition string, so under ASan `TEST_ATTRIB` aborts:

    ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... ParseAttribCondition (plink2_filter.cc:716) < Strchrnul < rawmemchr2

and the sanitizer build cannot run the suite past it. In a release build the over-read is normally harmless, but it can fault if the allocation ends on a page boundary.

### The fix

Pad the copy with `kBytesPerVec` zero bytes, the same treatment #445 gave the flattened string lists. This covers every current and future `CmdlineAllocString()` consumer rather than just the one call site.

### Testing

`TEST_ATTRIB` under `build_san`: aborts with the heap-buffer-overflow on master, passes with the fix. The whole 2.0 suite now runs to completion under ASan/UBSan ("All tests passed.", zero sanitizer reports), and the release build passes the full suite.

author: bryanfrd
body:
Closes #97.

The header search now opens the same list of matching tools as the home page, on every page, with the same debounce, the same loader and the same keyboard handling.

## Why it is not a Preact island

The obvious move is to reuse the island. I measured what that costs first: every page except the home currently ships **446 bytes** of JavaScript, the header script and nothing else. An island in the header adds preact and signals to all of them, roughly **8.6 KB gzipped**, on pages that today need no framework at all. For a site that was cut from 381 KB to 12.9 KB earlier in its life, paying nineteen times the current JS on every listing and content page to get a dropdown is the wrong trade.

So it is wired into the script the header already loads. The header script goes from 446 to **1383 bytes gzipped**, so **+937 bytes**, against +8.6 KB for the island.

## What is shared and what is not

The matching, ranking and URL building come from `suggest.ts`, which is already extracted and covered by nine tests, so the two call sites cannot drift on what counts as a match or how a target ranks. What is duplicated is the DOM and keyboard wiring, once in Preact and once by hand. That is the price of not shipping a framework, and it is the part a test would not have caught anyway.

The copy reaches the script through `data-` attributes on the field rather than a second translation source, so the four locales stay in the message catalogs, and the locale prefix is passed the same way, since the script has no access to `pathFor`.

## Checked in a browser

On `/fr/categories/`, typing "minecraft" returns all eight new entries with `/fr/` prefixes and Paper correctly offering its alternatives page rather than its own. `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded` and `aria-activedescendant` behave as on the home page, arrow keys and hover both move the selection, and the index is fetched exactly once.

`astro check` clean, build at 1264 pages, sitemap at 1260, which is the catalog refresh from #94 landing rather than anything here.

author: google-labs-stitch[bot]
body:
## Summary of Changes

This PR introduces AES-256-GCM encrypted envelope storage for Ed25519 identity private keys at rest, Argon2id key derivation from passphrases or machine identifiers, automatic mode 0600 file permission validation and enforcement, and backward-compatible migration for legacy unencrypted key files.

### Key Enhancements

1. **AES-256-GCM Envelope Encryption & Argon2id Key Derivation**
   - Stored identity key files now contain structured JSON envelopes (`KeyEnvelope`) with salt, nonce, Argon2id parameters, and AES-256-GCM encrypted ciphertext.
   - Key derivation checks passphrase environment variables (`CIPHER_IDENTITY_PASSPHRASE`, `CIPHER_PASSPHRASE`, `IDENTITY_PASSPHRASE`, `PASSPHRASE`) or resolves system machine IDs (`/etc/machine-id`, `/var/lib/dbus/machine-id`, or hostname/user fallback).

2. **Strict Mode 0600 Permission Enforcement**
   - Automatically checks file mode permissions on key loading.
   - Restricts permissive file modes (e.g. `0644` or `0777`) to `0600` before reading.

3. **Seamless Migration for Legacy Unencrypted Keys**
   - Automatically detects legacy unencrypted Ed25519 private key files and upgrades them to encrypted key vault envelopes during node initialization across all CLI entrypoints (`LoadOrCreate` and `LoadOrCreateFromPath`).
   - Uses atomic temporary file writes (`.tmp` file creation + `os.Rename`) to prevent key corruption during process crashes or disk write errors.

4. **Testing**
   - Expanded unit test coverage in `internal/identity/identity_test.go` covering envelope structure, permission enforcement, legacy migration, environment passphrases, and corrupt key handling.

author: mannyc2
body:
## Change

A cleanup observer that throws, defects, interrupts itself or never completes can no longer replace a successful canonical cleanup receipt with its own failed exit. Built-in Browserbase diagnostics and the optional `onCleanup` callback are independently bounded; a broken diagnostics reporter cannot prevent the callback from receiving the already-stored receipt. Teardown and provider release are still attempted once.

Implements [issue #66 WP5](https://github.com/mannyc2/effect-agent-browserbase/issues/66#issuecomment-5780803577), cleanup decision I and the Layer/receipt guidance in [#64 Part 4](https://github.com/mannyc2/effect-agent-browserbase/issues/64#issuecomment-5779390903). Stacked on WP4 (#70). This completes the implementation of WP0–WP5, the issue's publication gate; it does not publish the package set.

## Contract and compatibility

`reported` now delegates to the existing full-Exit `cleanupStep` with its two-second cooperative deadline. Both provider lifetimes and the Chromium lifetime defer callback construction inside that boundary. Receipt storage, Context-writer settlement and checked-close predicates remain outside it. Observer failure cannot mutate recorded cleanup facts, create a second release attempt, or turn unconfirmed cleanup into success.

No required public signature or schema changes. This is a behavioral correction: optional notification defects and interruption are contained instead of escaping the notification phase. Synchronous code that never yields remains outside cooperative timeout guarantees. Direct checked closure still returns the concrete cached receipt or fails with the existing typed error.

The guides and a compiled example distinguish a shared Layer-owned session from `Browser.scoped`. A Layer shares a finite lifetime and unchecked acquisition finalization; it does not independently supervise every consumer's fail-session errors. A bounded host-owned receipt sink outside an outer race preserves evidence even when the race returns `None` and discards the losing checked-close error. Body failure and direct/explicitly awaited exits retain the checked error in their own final cause.

## Regressions

Twenty-two new no-browser regressions use the actual owner, cleanup coordinator, source and scoped supervisor, with only native teardown and provider transport injected. They cover successful notification; construction throws; defects; self-interruption; notification timeout; receipt publication before notification; concurrent/repeated close with canonical object identity; one teardown and one owned release; borrowed cleanup without release; a failing ErrorReporter that does not suppress `onCleanup`; unchanged checked-close failure; and a canonical settlement failure that is not swallowed as an optional observer error.

The race regressions independently exercise outer `timeoutOption`, direct fiber interruption, body failure and explicitly awaited completion. They prove the exact surviving result/cause and one failed cleanup receipt in the host sink, followed by repeat reads/close without replay.

Source validation passed strict types for all three packages and integration, **472 unit/integration tests**, and all **113 source native tests** (browser 7, provider 80, Agent 26). Maintenance passed 141 tests with five existing Linux-only installer skips on macOS. New test type errors were fixed before execution: rc.115 `Fiber.interrupt` returns void, so the test explicitly awaits the final Exit; provider variants retain their distinct error channels instead of forcing a union through one generic inference. No diagnostic or regression was weakened.

## Final publication-gate evidence

Candidate: `b87a5d6c276c614c4459a46705c6c18c0737b4e9`.

The retained clean-candidate local **full** acceptance completed with raw exit **0**: **32/32 required stages** and **44/44 packed-consumer checks**. On resumption, the repository's `verifyStages` and `verifyReleaseSet` independently revalidated the stage inventory, source SHA, three tarball hashes/manifests and complete coordinated release receipt. The run is preserved at `/private/tmp/pr66-wp5-full-b87a5d6.IAJ4uw/results`; this recovery verification is not labeled as a new test execution.

All five installed consumers (`resources`, `browser`, `generic`, `agent`, `agent-hosted`) passed, including strict declarations/export parity, Node and Bun workflows and native package tests. Release identity, package dry-runs, upstream check/test/build and upstream release dry-run all returned raw zero. The verified local release-set SHA-256 is `8ef46a95fddf2e9e5d8736427f29f040adb8965b3b20fcf4bae330fa62454fd2`.

**Both current-head GitHub runs passed.** [PR Library CI](https://github.com/mannyc2/effect-agent-browserbase/actions/runs/35788438545) completed its 25 required stages and 44 packed-consumer checks. GitHub tested merge commit `4ee4b5f777e8938a166402d0d62dc6074b89828a`; its Git tree `574c1af2461c3f840a581a51e59e078fa37eb358` exactly matches this candidate. Linux maintenance ran 146 tests, with no failures or skips.

The deliberately dispatched **[full candidate CI](https://github.com/mannyc2/effect-agent-browserbase/actions/runs/35788447055)** checked exact source `b87a5d6c276c614c4459a46705c6c18c0737b4e9` and completed **32/32 required stages** and **44/44 packed-consumer checks**, all at raw zero. Both Unpaid acceptance and Native release recovery succeeded. Its downloaded artifact was verified with the repository's `verifyStages` and `verifyReleaseSet`: exact source, complete stage inventory, all consumer results, three tarball hashes/manifests and release-set identity. Acceptance artifact: `browserbase-acceptance-35788447055-1`, ID `10721524155`; remote release-set SHA-256: `161a4506294d8ffcf9e02ab336aec8c74fe0cb68c3baa97ccf33135bf4f85ad5`. author: gateway3b
body:
Two faults that showed up together as a white flash through every route transition, worst in dark mode. Reported in Media Mancer on both mobile and desktop, and reproducible in the playground.

## The document canvas ignored the theme

The theme is applied inline on the shell, which covers everything the shell paints. The document canvas is not covered:

- `g3-route-transitions` paints `html, body { background: var(--route-transition-bg, ...) }`, and g3-ui maps `--route-transition-bg` to `--g3-color-bg`.
- Every `::view-transition-*` pseudo-element is a child of `:root` and resolves that same variable there.

Both therefore took the stylesheet's **light default** no matter which theme was active, and the transition script then sampled that near-white `body` into `--route-transition-document-bg`, propagating it into the transition backdrop. One stale variable drove the whole flash.

Measured in the playground on the dark "Night" theme, before → after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `:root --g3-color-bg` | `#e9ebef` | `#07111f` |
| `:root --route-transition-bg` | `#e9ebef` | `#07111f` |
| `:root color-scheme` | `light` | `dark` |
| `body` / `html` background | `rgb(233,235,239)` | `rgb(7,17,31)` |

`AppWrapper` now mirrors the theme's background and `color-scheme` onto the document element. A nested `AppWrapper`, such as a demo frame inside a gallery, leaves it to the outermost one.

## A rail was never persistent chrome

`AdaptiveNav` and `NavRail` both documented the rail as persistent route-transition chrome — "it stays still while pages slide" — but the class was never applied. The rail sat inside the base region, so a routed sheet covered it and the live rail popped back when the transition ended.

`NavRail` is persistent at every width; `AdaptiveNav` only on wide shells, so a phone's bottom bar still rises under a sheet, which is the behaviour a sheet should have on a phone. Verified in the playground:

| viewport | nav | `view-transition-name` |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop | 64×548 rail | `persistent` |
| Mobile | 374×71 bar | `none` |

Pairs with g3-route-transitions 0.4.1, which stops a sheet from outranking persistent chrome.

All three strict clippy passes and the full test suite are green. The playground is relocked against the published g3-route-transitions 0.4.1.

author: jonahgabriel
body:
OMN-19194

market-drain measured (2026-09-22, OMN-17427 integration pass): the shadow
tests+coverage job's scoped slice (`-m "unit and not kafka"`) takes 621-663s
of pytest time plus ~90s of collection -- 711-753s total on a normal runner.
The old `--timeout 900` in `run_shadow_slice.py` left only 150-190s of
margin, and a ~25% slower runner (observed on PR #2777 at heads 544aa5abb
and 96c7c3e9e, and PR #2779 at af89283b0, plus merged PR #2773) pushed the
same correctly-scoped slice past the wall: exit 124. This step fell through
to the generic `failure` branch on that code, so `reason-graph` and
`product-readiness / evaluate` reported a false PRODUCT_FAILED root for a
runner-speed timeout, not a real product defect. Both contexts are
non-required, so nothing was blocked, but the report was wrong.

Two-part fix, mirroring the OMN-18820 exit-125 precedent already in this
file:
- raise the budget to 1200s -- 300s+ (27%+) margin over the worst-observed
  timed-out case;
- add an exit-124 branch reporting `product_conclusion=timeout` and
  succeeding the step, so a genuine remaining hang still routes to the
  infra dimension instead of a false PRODUCT_FAILED root.

This is a sibling fix under the same ticket as the onex_change_control
shadow-timeout fix (onex_change_control#10828, already merged) -- that repo's
shadow job was duplicating its full, unscoped test suite and needed
narrowing; this repo's shadow job was already correctly scoped and just
needed a realistic budget plus the same infra-classification the 125 case
already gets.

O cartão e a coluna “Já baixado” passaram a somar o histórico de baixas efetivadas, desconsiderando registros estornados. A mesma classificação por valor pago e saldo remanescente foi aplicada à vida do fornecedor, eliminando a divergência de contagem entre as duas telas.

O histórico expandido passou a exibir data, valor e conta de cada baixa também para notas quitadas. A ação de estorno foi disponibilizada tanto nessa listagem quanto no “Pagamento relacionado” do detalhe da nota em Fornecedores, respeitando a permissão existente. O fluxo exigiu motivo com pelo menos cinco caracteres, pediu confirmação explícita, preservou a baixa original no histórico e mostrou o código e o texto devolvidos pelo banco quando a operação foi recusada.

As funções `public.registrar_baixa_nota` e `public.estornar_baixa_nota`, suas migrations, a Programação Diária, processos e documentos não foram alterados.

Os testes de regras e integração passaram. O cenário crítico foi executado em Postgres isolado com AUTO POSTO GLOBO LTDA, nota 296.771 e conta 2.042-7 FPM: registrou baixa parcial, quitou a nota, reabriu-a por estorno, recompôs o saldo no centavo e preservou o lançamento original. A idempotência do segundo estorno e a exclusão de estornos dos totais também foram verificadas pela suíte. A sintaxe JSX de todas as telas modificadas foi validada sem gerar artefatos de build.

author: stormer78
body:
Adds `vtc/vetting/vetters/show/0.1`. This is the spec half of OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1651, which came from Keyring's VTI-Q3.

## Why

`vtc/vetting/vetters/list` omits a vetter with no published profile and a vetter whose grant was revoked in exactly the same way: both are simply absent. So:

- an applicant mid-exchange with a vetter who has gone quiet cannot tell whether that vetter was removed or never chose to be listed;
- a vetter cannot check their own standing at all.

The only way to find out today is to read the grant credential's own status list, which requires already holding the credential.

## What it answers

By DID: `live`, `revoked`, `expired` or `none`, plus `grantId`, the timestamp that ended or will end it, and — for a live grant — `listed`, which is what separates "a vetter who chose not to be listed" from "not a vetter".

A **new task** rather than a `status` member on the listing response: adding a member to an existing response is breaking for consumers that reject unknown members, and the two answer different questions — the listing is discovery, this is a lookup about someone you can already name.

## Three judgement calls worth reviewing

1. **`revoked` outranks `expired`** where both hold. Withdrawal and lapse are different statements about the community's trust, and an applicant reads them differently.
2. **`none` does not distinguish a non-member from a member who is not a vetter.** The caller asked about vetting; membership is not theirs to learn here. Conformance also asks that the answer cost the same whatever the status, so timing does not leak what the payload withholds.
3. **The revocation reason is not carried**, including through `ext`, which the Security & Privacy section says explicitly. It is the community's internal record and frequently concerns a third party; the caller needs to know the grant does not hold.

The response is also deliberately *not* evidence: a grant can be revoked a second after the answer is sent, so the spec says a `live` answer must not be treated as durable proof of eligibility — that is what the vetter's credential in `vetting/request` is for.

## Checks

- `npm run validate`: 473 specs, no errors, and no warning against this spec.
- `npm run build`: passes; all three examples validate against the framework envelope.
- Bindings regenerated for **Rust, TypeScript and Go** — the Go drift check in `.github/workflows/go.yml` makes that third one required, though the contributing guide lists only two.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs`: passes.
- No version bumps and no changelog entries, per RELEASING.md — the Release PR assigns those.

author: martinambrus
body:
Four merged PRs built it (#210, #215, #216, #217) and `AGENTS.md` said nothing about it — the word "untrusted" appears once in the whole file, about grok's folder trust. Everything was in commit messages and docblocks, which is where a reader looks last.

## What the section states that the code cannot

- **Why four variants rather than one.** The blocks share a first half; the **ending** is the choice, and it has to match what the pass's output can carry. A reporting duty handed to a pass whose findings array holds one kind of thing arrives as a fake finding — `04a`/`05` would file a prompt-injection report as a **spec defect**, and `05a`'s corrector would then edit the spec in response to something it read in a source file.
- **Why the persona carve-out is in all four, and why it governs METHOD.** `agentDefinitionGuidance` points an agent at the repo's own definition, so a block saying nothing under `.claude/` is an instruction contradicts the file the same prompt just named. The limit is the half that is easy to omit: a persona says HOW to work, never what you may find.
- **Why fencing is not belt-and-braces over the guards.** `REPO_IS_DATA_LINES` *requires* its reviewer to quote the hostile string with its file and line, so hostile content reaches the next prompt **by design**. One validator's output needed three fences.

## Two rules, each of which cost several rounds to find

> **Fence where a person's words and a machine's are JOINED. Balance wherever the result is CUT.**

Plus the line nobody should have to rediscover: **never fence the operator**, because a fence is containment for agent prose and sabotage for a person's.

## Three failure modes, now design constraints rather than anecdotes

- An assertion over a step's **concatenated** prompts passes as soon as one arm carries the guard.
- A **hand-enumerated** set of plan writers missed the two living under `workflow/`; the set is derived from `PLAN_PATCH_CONTRACT`.
- Anything applied in `detect()` never reaches a step detected before it shipped.

Docs only. No code, no behaviour, no tests. `prettier --check` clean.

body:
Closes the first two parts of #2664 (the `:landed` kind and set check deriving done from criteria, with `done=` / `percent=`). Part 3 (the session asks) is not in this PR. **What.** - `:kind :landed :subject "pr:#" :predicate :merged-or-closed-in-base` (`:landed-in` is accepted as the same predicate). It holds in three cases: - the PR is **merged**; - the PR is **closed and the lander's rule holds**: `git merge-tree --write-tree ` yields the base's own tree, meaning merging the PR changes nothing. This is checked at the base tip first. If the tip fails, it is checked at each first-parent base commit between the head's commit and one hour after the PR closed. The lander's own commit lies in that window. Example: #2625's merge conflicts at dev's tip because a later landing rewrote what it added, but changes nothing at 63eea6f3. - the subject is `commit:` and that commit is **reachable from the base**. - The merge runs in one blobless bare repo per repo under `--cache` (default `/nova-work/landed`). Fetches use gh as the credential helper: the base once per run, then `refs/pull//head` for each PR. It is blobless rather than shallow because merge-tree needs the merge base. PR metadata comes through the `gh` seam (`Runner`), and each question is asked once per run. Anything that cannot be answered prints `holds=unknown` and counts as not done. - `nova-work set check --file [--evaluate] [--base ] [--cache ] [--write-status]`: - Every run prints `SET DONE done= percent=

` after `SET OK`, with percent rounded down. - `--evaluate` takes done from the criteria (`:landed` and `:merged :merged-at`) instead of `:status`, and prints one `SET EVAL` line per criterion. The base is required: `--base`, else the set's `:base`. - `--write-status` changes `:status "open"` to `"landed"` where every criterion holds. It touches only those bytes. - The help text, docs/CLI.md and the SPEC-WORKLANG A14 amendment are updated. **Dogfood** (real gh, on #2665's set with `:merged-at` rewritten to `:landed`): `SET DONE done=28 percent=66`. All six closed-as-landed PRs hold, and so do the two controls: **#2544** (combined with #2614 in #2629) and **#2645** (combined into #2670). No single dev commit carries either one's files byte for byte. **Tests** use no network: gh is faked, and the forge's git repo is built in `t.TempDir()` and fetched over `file://`. They cover: - a merged PR counts as done - the #2544 shape counts as done: two PRs combined into one landing commit, then dev moves on - a closed PR whose content a later commit rewrote is done at its landing commit (the #2625 shape), and not done without a landing window - a never-landed PR is not done (`merge-changes-base`) - a conflicting PR is not done (`merge-conflicts`) - an open PR is not done - a closed PR under `:merged-at` is not done - no cache or unreachable gh gives unknown - each question reaches gh once per run, and the cache is reused across runs - base refusal and override - percent arithmetic - `--write-status` changes exactly one line per flipped unit and is idempotent `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test ./...` is green. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

author: diberry
body:
## Summary

Fixes the ADME (Azure Data Manager for Energy) CLI tab generation bug: `config/namespace-mapping.json` — the namespace allowlist/configuration file — was missing an `"adme"` entry, causing generated ADME articles to have 8 tool H2 sections but 0 Azure CLI / Azure MCP Server tab groups. This required a manual hand-repair in MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs-pr#9827 (commit `3b43c0f2a6001592d86cbe939b38486638ecc282`) to restore 8 Azure CLI tabs and 8 Azure MCP Server tabs.

Closes #831

## Root cause

- `mcp-tools/data/brand-to-server-mapping.json` already correctly maps `adme` -> `azure-data-manager-for-energy` (added in commit `0d092d2`, the beta.44 bump).
- `config/namespace-mapping.json` (the namespace allowlist/configuration gate, ~58 entries) was **missing the corresponding `adme` entry** despite covering essentially every other active namespace.
- The beta.44 CLI metadata (`mcp-cli-metadata/3.0.0-beta.44+.../cli-output.json`) contains exactly 8 real `adme`-prefixed CLI commands.

## Fix

Smallest repository-pattern change: add `"adme": "azure-data-manager-for-energy.md"` to `config/namespace-mapping.json`, matching the existing pattern used for all other entries in that file. No changes to the gating/allowlist code itself.

## Test evidence

Added `mcp-tools/DocGeneration.Steps.ToolFamilyCleanup.Tests/AdmeCliTabGenerationTests.cs`, a regression test proving:
1. `config/namespace-mapping.json` contains an `adme` entry consistent with `brand-to-server-mapping.json`.
2. `CliTabConfig` admits the `adme` namespace.
3. Using the real committed beta.44 `cli-output.json` fixture (8 `adme` tools), `CliTabWrapper.ApplyTabsToFamilyArticle` emits **exactly 8 Azure CLI tabs and 8 Azure MCP Server tabs**, with no malformed/unpaired tab groups.

```
Passed!  - Failed: 0, Passed: 3, Skipped: 0, Total: 3, Duration: 126 ms - DocGeneration.Steps.ToolFamilyCleanup.Tests.dll (net10.0)
```

Before the fix, the first test (`NamespaceMappingAllowlist_ContainsAdme_MatchingBrandMapping`) failed with:
```
config/namespace-mapping.json is the namespace allowlist/configuration gate and must contain an 'adme' entry
(it was previously absent, causing 0 CLI/MCP tab groups to be generated for the ADME article).
```

Full existing suite (`dotnet test` in `DocGeneration.Steps.ToolFamilyCleanup.Tests`) run before and after this change: **973 passed / 6 failed both before and after** (verified via `git stash` on unmodified `main`). The 6 failures are pre-existing and unrelated to this change:
- 2 failures are an environment-specific path-length issue (`RegressionTestHelpers.FindRepoRoot()` mishandles the Windows extended-length `\\?\` path prefix that .NET reports for this deeply-nested isolated worktree clone path) affecting unrelated `CliTabConfigGenerationTests` cases. The new `AdmeCliTabGenerationTests` in this PR intentionally avoids this shared helper's fragile path-walk to remain robust in this environment.
- 4 failures are pre-existing `ToolReaderMultiTokenNamespaceTests` failures unrelated to CLI tab generation.

No AI credentials were required for this fix or its test — the deterministic rendering stage (`CliTabWrapper`, `CliTabConfig`) was tested directly using committed fixture data.

## Links

- ADO work item: https://dev.azure.com/msft-skilling/Content/_workitems/edit/633623
- Content PR that required hand-repair: MicrosoftDocs/azure-dev-docs-pr#9827

## Not included

- No merge performed; opening for review per process.
- The 8-agent review is intentionally NOT run by this PR — the coordinator will run it separately.

author: gabrieljablonski
body:
Closes #708

## O que muda

- **`knowledge_document_get`** e **`knowledge_document_update`**: as ferramentas do MCP para `GET` e `PATCH /v1/knowledge/documents/:id`. A leitura traz o texto inteiro, que antes não era alcançável de lugar nenhum pelo MCP. A edição mantém o id; só um texto que mudou é re-embedado, e a prévia (padrão, `dry_run` desligado só por pedido) diz se vai reindexar pela mesma pergunta que o serviço faz, recusa o texto que o banco não guarda, como o apply recusaria (rodada 1 do review), e recusa título ou texto vazio, como a REST (`minLength: 1`) já recusa, porque um texto vazio apagaria o conteúdo e o ingest seguinte derrubaria os chunks (rodada 3). A auditoria é a que o serviço já escrevia para a REST (`knowledge_document.update`).
- **`limit` e `cursor` em `GET /v1/knowledge/bases/:id/documents` e em `knowledge_documents_list`**. O `limit` era aceito e ignorado nas duas portas (comentário da issue). Agora pagina, mais novos primeiro, e a resposta traz `nextCursor`. Sem `limit` a base inteira vem como sempre veio, com `nextCursor: null`. `limit` inválido e `cursor` que não é um cursor dão 400 nomeando o parâmetro, em vez de recomeçar do topo. O cursor carrega a própria posição (`<createdAt ms>_<id>`), então apagar o documento em que uma página parou não interrompe a leitura, que é o caso de um sync editando a base enquanto a lê.
- **`src/modules/mcp/route-coverage.ts`**: as 213 rotas de `src/api/v1/*.controller.ts`, cada uma com uma de três respostas: a ferramenta que a cobre (120), `none` com o motivo (68: corpo binário, passo de OAuth, o próprio transporte, operação de SUPER_ADMIN irreversível ou que cunha credencial, segredo cunhado, seletores do console), ou `gap`, que é rota que deveria ter ferramenta e ainda não tem (25, escritas por extenso). A rodada 2 do review achou oito rotas de frota que eu tinha marcado como sem par porque listei as ferramentas sem o escopo `mcp:admin`; o teste agora lista com ele. `tests/modules/mcp-route-coverage.test.ts` reprova rota nova sem entrada, entrada de rota que sumiu, e `tool` que não existe no servidor, dizendo método e caminho. `docs/mcp.md` aponta para o arquivo.

## Sobre o escopo

O comentário da issue sugeria tratar o `limit` ignorado em outra issue. Entrou aqui porque apareceu na mesma investigação e o conserto é pequeno. Só honrar o `limit` não bastaria: um sync receberia uma lista cortada sem saber que está cortada, por isso veio com cursor, na convenção das outras listas do repo.

As 25 lacunas ficam como lacunas: o que a issue pede é que elas fiquem visíveis e que a CI cobre o delta, não que todas virem ferramenta nesta PR.

## Prova

- `tests/modules/mcp-knowledge-document-tools.test.ts`: leitura com texto, outro tenant não alcança, prévia não muda nada e diz se reindexa (inclusive com o texto igual ao atual), edição só de título não reindexa, edição de texto mantém o id, reenfileira e audita, pedido vazio recusado até na prévia, token só de leitura não edita, paginação completa sem repetir nem pular, sem `limit` a base inteira, cursor forjado e `limit` 0 recusados, e o documento do cursor apagado entre páginas sem interromper a leitura.
- `tests/modules/mcp-route-coverage.test.ts`: as quatro regras acima, mais a garantia de que a varredura acha as rotas (inclusive as duas escritas como `}).post(`).
- `tests/api/v1/query-filter-refusal.test.ts` ganha `limit=abc` e `cursor=abc` na rota de documentos.
- Prova vermelha na base (`49863d89`): as recusas de `limit`/`cursor` falham e os arquivos novos não carregam; com o arquivo de cobertura copiado para a base, o teste de paridade reprova apontando exatamente `GET` e `PATCH /v1/knowledge/documents/:id`.
- Mutação 13/14 mortos. O sobrevivente tira o `LIMIT` do SQL: a página continua certa, porque o corte também acontece em memória, e o que se perde é só ler mais linhas do que precisa.
- Duas cercas do repo atualizadas com o motivo: o teto de tamanho do `tools/list` (medido: base 30.447/57.193, esta árvore 30.729/57.777) e a tabela de coerência de dry-run, que ganha `knowledge_document_update`. O `rows.slice(0, take)` entra na lista de cortes de array da varredura de cortes crus.
- `bun check` completo: 12258 pass, 4 skip, 0 fail.

author: eersnington
akinfold
body:
## What

A new `install`-marked suite in `tests/install/` installs the plugin into a **real Hermes**, by every route the README documents, and asks Hermes what it loaded. Nothing is simulated:

- Each test lays out a home directory the way the official Hermes installer does: the Hermes checkout and its virtualenv under `~/.hermes/hermes-agent`, Hermes' own `uv` at `~/.hermes/bin/uv`, the `hermes` launcher in `~/.local/bin`.
- It runs the README's commands as written, with `HOME` pointing there. The only departures: the Git install adds `--ref <commit under test>`, the PyPI install names the wheel about to be published, and the drop-in archive is the one about to be attached to the release.
- A route passes only if `hermes plugins list` shows the plugin as enabled, Hermes' plugin manager loads it without error at the expected version, and all seven tools are in the agent's catalog. Hermes leaves a tool out of that catalog when its availability check fails, so a tool counts only when its credentials are visible to Hermes.
- The Git route also checks that the install asked for both credentials and saved the answers to `~/.hermes/.env`. The drop-in route also runs the README's `defusedxml` remedy. The fourth test checks that installing from the repository root still behaves the way the README warns.

`test_readme_gives_the_commands_under_test` runs with the unit tests and fails if the README and the suite stop giving the same commands.

The **Install check** workflow runs the four routes against the latest Hermes release and against Hermes `main` (the installer's default), eight jobs. `ci.yml` calls it on every pull request, and `release-publish.yml` runs it on the artifacts it just built: the GitHub Release and the PyPI upload now `need` it.

## What it found, fixed here

1. **The Git install never asked for credentials.** `requires_env` entries used `key`/`prompt`. Hermes reads `name` (plus `description`, `url`, `secret`) and drops entries without a `name`. So the prompt the README promised never appeared. Fixed, and the password is now `secret: true`.
2. **`pip install hermes-yandex-calendar` does not reach Hermes**, and neither does the README's `pip install 'defusedxml>=0.7'` remedy. The installer builds Hermes' virtualenv with `uv` and without `pip`, so the `pip` on `PATH` installs into some other Python. The README now gives commands that install into that virtualenv, enables with `hermes plugins enable yandex_calendar`, and spells out the drop-in `unzip`. It also says that Option A, like Option C, installs no dependencies. A standard Hermes already has `defusedxml`, pulled in through one of the extras its installer includes. If Hermes ever drops it, this suite fails on the Git and drop-in routes.

All four routes pass locally on Hermes v0.21.4 and on `main`.

## Live e2e on the Hermes users have

The **E2E (live)** workflow installed `hermes-agent` from PyPI. That package stopped at 0.19.0, while Hermes moved on to 0.21 through tagged GitHub releases. When the install failed, `continue-on-error` let the run go on without Hermes. So the live suite never exercised the Hermes users actually run, and a missing Hermes looked like a pass.

- Setting up Hermes the way its installer does now lives in a local action, `.github/actions/setup-hermes`, shared by the install check and the e2e workflow.
- The e2e workflow sets Hermes up with it, installs the plugin into Hermes' own Python 3.11 virtualenv, and runs the suite with that interpreter.
- A `hermes` choice input picks the latest release (default), `main`, or `none`, which keeps the plugin's stand-ins.
- With Hermes, the run fails if the plugin cannot import it, instead of silently testing the stand-ins.

`hermes plugins compat` on Hermes v0.21.4 and on `main` reports that the plugin imports nothing scheduled for removal. `agent.web_search_provider.get_provider_env`, the one Hermes entry point every plugin in the family uses, is still defined there.

author: aworthysg
body:
Two reported bugs.

## 1. Edited progress reports reverted to their old text

The editor was not at fault. **Save Changes** dispatches `UPDATE_REPORT`, the reducer merges it, and the viewer shows the new text. The edit was lost **afterwards**, in the Firebase sync.

`useFirebaseSync` treats Firebase as authoritative on load: `MERGE_FIREBASE_STATE` replaces each local array with the Firebase copy. The write back to Firebase is debounced by 2 s. So:

- **Save, then reload within 2 s** → localStorage (300 ms) holds the edit, Firebase does not → the load replaces it with the stale copy → the next write pushes the stale text back up, and the edit is gone for good.
- **Save on an iPhone, then switch app** → iOS suspends the tab's timers, the write never fires, the tab is later reloaded → same result. The reported upload screenshot was taken on iPhone Safari, so this path is the likely one.
- **The write fails for any reason** → it was only logged via `console.error`, so nobody saw it, and every later load restored the old text.

Reproduced against the real reducer before changing anything:

```
after save, in memory : EDITED BY TUTOR
after reload + merge  : ORIGINAL TEXT (edit LOST)
```

### Fix

- **Per-report merge, newest wins.** `ADD_REPORT`, `UPDATE_REPORT`, `SHARE_REPORT` and `UNSHARE_REPORT` stamp `updatedAt`. `MERGE_FIREBASE_STATE` now routes `reports` through `mergeReports`, which keeps whichever copy of each report is newer. A report on only one side is kept. An unstamped copy predates this change and loses to any stamped one. On a tie, the Firebase copy wins, which matches the old behaviour. Reports have no delete action, so keeping one-sided records cannot resurrect a deletion. **Every other array keeps wholesale replacement.** Arrays that support deletion (`resources`, `events`, `posts`) must not get this merge; `CLAUDE.md` now says so.
- **Flush on hide.** `useFirebaseSync` sends the pending write straight away on `visibilitychange` (hidden) and `pagehide`, which closes the 2 s window for every kind of edit, not just reports.
- A `null` `reports` payload from Firebase used to set `reports` to `null`, which would crash every `.filter`. It now leaves the list intact.

### Verification

Ten merge scenarios against the real reducer, all passing:

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Local edit vs stale Firebase copy (the reported bug) | local kept |
| Newer edit from another device | still arrives |
| Both edited | later stamp wins |
| Unsynced new report | kept |
| Report added on another device | arrives |
| Legacy tie, both unstamped | Firebase copy wins, as before |
| Indexed-object payload `{"0":…}` | rebuilt to an array |
| `null` payload | list intact |
| Share vs stale copy | share kept |
| Other arrays (`posts`) | still replaced wholesale |

End to end in Chromium on the real Progress page with the real reducer: open a report → Edit → type → Save Changes → reopen (edit shown) → replay the app's reload sequence with a stale Firebase copy → **edit kept**. No page errors.

## 2. Privacy Policy link was broken

Settings → About linked to `/privacy`, which never had a page. `vercel.json` rewrites every path to `index.html`, and the app has no `/privacy` route, so the link bounced to the dashboard. It was added that way in 29e7522.

The company publishes its policy at **`a-worthy.com/privacy-policy/`** (A-Worthy Pte Ltd, PDPA, DPO `hello@aworthy.sg`). The link now opens that page. `vercel.json` also redirects `/privacy` and `/privacy-policy` on this domain to the same URL, so old bookmarks and shared links resolve. Redirects run before the SPA rewrite, and the service worker passes the navigation request straight through, so the browser follows the 308.

**Scope note:** that policy is written for the marketing site. It covers enquiry forms, WhatsApp and Plausible analytics. It does not mention what the LMS processes: homework submissions, grades, attendance, progress reports, uploaded files, or the submission text sent to Anthropic for AI marking. Extending it is a decision for the business, not a code change.

## Checks

- `npm run lint` — 0 problems
- `npm run build` — clean
- Service worker cache bumped to v46

body:
## Summary

#793's route warm-up step (PR #803) only mined `page.goto('/...')` targets. API routes hit via `request.get/post/put/delete()` or `fetch` from within test helpers (e.g. `sendWebhook` posting to `/api/webhooks/monnify`) are compiled independently by Next.js and are just as cold on first hit — producing the same "different unrelated test failing each run" pattern #793 diagnosed, just scoped to `/api/` instead of pages.

Confirmed against **PR #839**'s actual `E2E Regression Suite` failure (critical tier, 14.2 min, unrelated to that PR's REQ-108 diff): the warmed route list produced by this fix includes `/api/admin/settings/points-conversion-rate/impact` — the exact endpoint whose cold first-hit produced an `ECONNRESET` in that run, alongside an unrelated menu-card visibility timeout in `express-order-portion-pricing-req097.spec.ts` (same class of cold-compile symptom).

## Scope note

This is deliberately narrower than the full fix that might eventually be needed for issue #832 (576-test / ~38min full-regression tier, hypothesized connection/state pressure accumulating over a long single-worker run). This PR targets the `critical` tier's cold-compile gap specifically; #832's longer-running-tier theory (e.g. sharding with periodic server restarts) is a separate, bigger follow-up not conflated with this change.

- [x] YAML validated (`python3 -c "import yaml; yaml.safe_load(...)"`)
- [x] Confirmed the warmed-route list includes the exact endpoint that failed in PR #839
- [ ] `workflow_dispatch` scoped verification run (in progress)

author: animatedgtvr
body:
Adds a resource preflight before Pippin builds/boots and turns the launch terminal into a persistent diagnostic console while the desktop is running.

Host preflight:
- new `scripts/preflight.sh` reads Linux host CPU model, logical threads, total RAM, and free project-disk space
- writes calculated values to `build/pippin-limits.env`
- selects constrained/balanced/comfortable/high profiles
- calculates QEMU RAM at 256/384/512/768 MiB based on host RAM
- intentionally caps QEMU below Pippin's current 1 GiB early direct-map boundary
- calculates compiler parallelism while reserving host headroom, capped at 8 jobs
- warns for <2 GiB RAM or <1 GiB free disk
- `make specs` prints the calculation without booting
- normal kernel and ISO builds run preflight first and use its build-job limit

Runtime diagnostics:
- `run-qemu.sh` sources the calculated QEMU memory limit
- creates `build/logs/runtime.log`, `shell.log`, and `qemu-debug.log`
- keeps guest serial output visible in the host terminal as `[guest]`
- keeps C# shell stdout/stderr visible as `[shell]` / `[shell:err]`
- keeps QEMU stderr visible as `[qemu]`
- enables QEMU `guest_errors` diagnostics and mirrors them live as `[qemu-debug]`
- logs remain available after the desktop/QEMU session exits

This is intended to make resource-related failures and GUI/bridge/kernel faults visible instead of disappearing when Pippin switches into the graphical desktop.

author: hnegi01
body:
Two changes that both need to reach the host, released together.

## Security (#37)

Seven fixes from an adversarial review of this public repo. **No secrets were ever committed** — 1,684 blobs across 6 branches and 237 commits came back clean. What was wrong is controls that were advisory, failed open, or that a supported setting silently disabled, with documentation asserting the opposite in three places.

- **The approval gate was forgeable.** The key is a pure function of `(tool_id, args)` and the API took it on trust, so any client could compute one, skip the dialog, and have the write logged as approved. Now bound to dialogs the server actually issued, per session, with a TTL.
- **Warehouse credentials were written to disk in cleartext.** The MCP scrubber exact-matched where the backend substring-matched, so `aws_secret_key`, `db_password`, `client_secret` and `private_key` were logged verbatim into the always-on mutation audit.
- **The audit trail was level-gated** — `FES_LOG_LEVEL=WARNING` silently discarded it.
- **The allowlist failed open** on an unreadable file, exposing 20 extra write tools on one bad byte.
- **Skill resume skipped plan validation**, and the **skill answer path leaked result data** with summarization off.
- **Supply chain:** 14 actions pinned to SHAs, CD dropped to `contents: read` with write scoped to the tagging job, publishing gated on `main`, version validated as semver, Dependabot config and a security policy added.

**CD now waits for CI.** Both workflows fired on the same push and neither waited for the other, so a commit with failing tests still published `:latest`. A `verify` job runs ruff and both engines inside CD, and `push-images` needs it.

## nginx (#38)

The Meta-Management MCP stack's routing was a hand edit on the box, so every `git pull` wiped it or conflicted. Now in the repo, with the upstream resolved at **request** time via a variable and Docker's embedded resolver.

A literal `proxy_pass` is resolved at config **load**, so a missing MCP stack would stop nginx starting at all and take this app down with it — which is what happened on 2026-09-21. Verified across nine cases, including a full nginx restart with the stack absent.

`nginx/default.conf` is bind-mounted from the checkout, so it ships on `git pull` and needs no image.

## Tests

879 on both engines, up from 693.

## After merge

The host is on **2.7.1**; 2.7.2 was built but never deployed. This supersedes it.

## What

Observation 18 — **A Correction Inherits the Frame It Corrects**. The research behind PRs #12 and #14, written because the sequence is one defect at three levels rather than three defects.

[Observation 14](https://github.com/dan-petty/vibes/blob/main/observations/systems/14-defect-shaped-loops-and-the-feature-blind-spot.md) found the loop could only see defects. The landscape survey was the correction — and it declared four capabilities, all four linters, with **thirteen of sixteen sample applications absent from its manifest**. Every one of the thirteen gaps it emitted was therefore a linter feature, and the top-ranked one was a well-cited proposal to make the linter more like `ruff`.

The narrowing survived the correction by moving out of the code and into the manifest, which is code that nothing executes. It also arrived carrying verified upstream citations, and a citation lends its rigour to the *choice* as well as to the claim.

The balance metric added to detect the drift then did the same thing one level down. Over one fixed window of twenty commits, re-measured for this write-up:

| factory commit `112ba87` | by location | 350 | 5,692 | 6% |
| factory commit `112ba87` | by declaration | 862 | 5,692 | 15% |

The numerator did not move. 512 lines of application factory landed and capability investment stayed at exactly 350.

- Corrects **"twelve of sixteen" to thirteen** in `AGENTS.md` §1 and `CHANGELOG.md`. The original manifest held four capability entries but named only three distinct sample applications, because one of the four paths was `tools/docs_validator.py`.

author: thclark
body:
Third PR of the `gpu-canvas` trunk, stacked on #46 (`gpu-canvas-2d`); retarget to `gpu-canvas` once #46 merges. It delivers the last of #13: strokes expanded on the GPU and markers as instances of one outline.

## Strokes

- **One segment per edge.** A stroked path is flattened into a polyline in its own item space and uploaded as `Segment` instances (64 bytes each) with their neighbours, arc lengths and depths; the width, cap, join, dashes, colour and item-to-figure transform go into a `StrokeParams` slot bound with a dynamic offset per draw. lyon's stroker for paths, the dash splitter and the `lyon_algorithms` dependency are gone.
- **Expanded in the shaders.** The vertex shader builds the body, the join (miter within the PDF limit of four, else bevel, or an arc) and the caps of every segment; the fragment shader dashes by arc length with the caps of the stroke on every dash, cut at the subpath's ends and anti-aliased, and takes each dash as half-open so a corner at a dash's start joins whole and one at its end does not. Around a joint of a dashed stroke with round or square caps, a fan is drawn whose coverage the dashes on each adjacent segment decide, because those caps reach where a join would. Widths transform with the geometry (an anisotropic pen under a non-uniform transform, as in PDF), a hairline is one screen point in every direction, and a zero-length dash is a dot with round caps and nothing otherwise, as PDF 32000 has it.
- **No self-blending.** A stroke outside a depth group is depth-tested against itself at a depth of its own, falling with every such stroke since the last depth clear, so a translucent polyline has no dark specks at its joints, as it has none in PDF. Inside a depth group a stroke takes its segments' depths and follows its face's plane across its width; its overlaps may blend twice, which is documented.
- **Verified against poppler.** Every join × cap × dash pattern of a zigzag, and dashed closed outlines around their seam, are rendered offscreen and compared with `pdftoppm`'s raster of the same display list exported to PDF, within the tolerances of the dense-surface exports; probe tests pin the miter limit, single blending, hairlines, dash phase and anti-aliasing, caps, the anisotropic pen, a stroke after a depth group and two crossing strokes.

## Markers

- **One item per artist or run.** `ItemKind::Markers` holds the outline of the marker shape in unit space, the edge width and one `MarkerInstance` per marker (position, size, depth, face and edge colours, data index). The compiler pushes one marker per item, sorts a 3D axes as before, then merges every run the sort leaves together, so the painter's order is unchanged; in 2D an artist's markers are one item.
- **PDF unchanged, viewer instanced.** The exporter writes one path per instance; the viewer tessellates the outline once (its edge with lyon's stroker at a nominal width, recording the offset of every edge vertex so the edge is exactly as wide as the item says at every instance size) and draws the instances through one instanced draw, fill before edge.
- The display-list types were reviewed on this PR before they were built.

## Verification

- `IRONLAB_REQUIRE_BUF=1 IRONLAB_REQUIRE_PDF_TOOLS=1 IRONLAB_REQUIRE_GPU=1 cargo test --workspace`, clippy with `-D warnings` and `pre-commit run --all-files` pass locally on Metal; the docs build strictly.
- Every gallery figure re-rendered through the new pipelines stays within a few levels of 255 per block of the render before this PR, and the viewer was opened on line- and marker-heavy figures without a panic or a validation error.

author: alexanderolelife
body:
Tres cambios contra la misma fricción. El motor ya tenía dos mecanismos para ahorrarle memoria al PM: uno estaba roto y el otro no existía.

## 1. Disparadores desambiguados

Las listas de frases se habían copiado entre secciones del skill, así que ocho frases disparaban dos o tres verbos distintos.

| Antes | Después |
|---|---|
| 47 frases, 8 ambiguas | 47 frases, 0 ambiguas |

«reconciliá X con el cerebro» podía caer en `roadmap`, `sync` o `reconciliar`. No es un problema de memoria del usuario: el despacho era una moneda al aire.

## 2. El slug deja de ser un requisito de memoria

`intake-resolve.mjs` resuelve por slug exacto, clave de la épica, prefijo, parte del slug o palabras del título, tolerando acentos y espacios. Sin consulta toma el último intake tocado, o el único activo.

```
"poliza"                       → ambiguo: lista los 3 candidatos (código 2)
"SO-912"                       → modulo-poliza-petra  (clave de la épica)
"el modulo de poliza de petra" → modulo-poliza-petra  (palabras del título)
""                             → el último que tocaste
```

Nunca adivina entre varios: devuelve los candidatos para que el skill pregunte o abra el panel.

## 3. Verbo `siguiente`

Responde «¿y ahora qué?» con el estado que el intake ya tiene calculado, y propone **una** acción con el porqué en números:

```
🗿 modulo-poliza-petra · draft — 23/23 historias entregadas · 118 dudas abiertas

  Lo que sigue:  /argos-product:intake preguntar modulo-poliza-petra
  Por qué:       57 duda(s) abiertas que contradicen el PRD o preguntan a Producto,
                 todavía sin llevar al canal
```

Solo lee: no toca Jira, Slack ni Confluence, y lo que escribe afuera conserva su compuerta.

## De paso

`next-step` cuenta como fuera de juego una historia tachada o con el estado anotado, por ejemplo «**descartada** (decision-log #50)», que comparando por igualdad exacta se contaba como viva.

## Verificación

CI local en verde: 9 tests unitarios (uno nuevo cubre las diez formas de resolver un slug) y el smoke con 5 asserts nuevos. Probado además contra los 10 intakes reales del repo de datos.

author: quantumplation
body:
`QueryProviderSundaeSwap` mapped `liquidity.lpTotal` from `current.quantityLP`, which is the **circulating** LP supply. Every v4 curve module divides by the pool datum's `total_lp` — circulating plus the protocol's earned-but-unharvested fees — and concentrated liquidity uses it as its liquidity term `L`. So a v4 deposit, withdrawal or CL swap quoted from a pool this provider returned was computed against a different pool than the chain validates.

## Is this a crash?

**No, and I want to correct that up front, because I raised it as one.** In review on #175 I repeated a claim that six of eight v4 pools on preview report zero circulating LP, and that this divides by zero rather than merely under-estimating. I inherited that claim from a comment in another repository and passed it on without checking it. Both halves are wrong:

- **No v4 pool has zero circulating LP.** 0 of 17 sampled across preview and preprod.
- **Nothing divides by zero.** At `lpTotal = 0` the v4 deposit and CL-swap paths throw clear errors, and `ConstantProductPool.getTokensForLp` does not fault either — `Fraction` treats a zero denominator as 1, so it returns a silently absurd answer instead. Worth knowing, but not reachable and not a crash.

So this is a **correctness bug, not a crash**. It is still worth fixing, because the numbers are wrong in a direction that is not safely conservative.

## Measured impact

17 live v4 pools, preview and preprod. 15 carry a nonzero gap:

| pool | curve | relative error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c87d5c55fda8` (preview) | constant_sum | 0.1586% |
| `02d4780d8a47` (preview) | constant_sum | 0.1399% |
| `ba6b17dc192a` (preview) | constant_sum | 0.1358% |
| `b3cc21fb7218` (preview) | constant_sum | 0.1265% |
| `ac8d4b1b5fca` (preview) | stableswap | 0.0007% |
| `bdde12e15189` (preprod) | constant_sum | 0.0191% |

The direction is not uniform across operations: the wrong denominator **understates** minted LP on a deposit and **overstates** the tokens a withdrawal returns. The second is the user-facing one — quoting more than the chain will pay.

## Why this is uniform and not version-aware

This touches every contract version, so the question is whether v1/v3 genuinely want circulating LP. They do not want a *different* number — they want the same one.

The API documents it: *"For pre-v4 pools there is no separate fee accounting, so this equals `current.quantityLP`."*

Documentation is a claim, so I measured it: **222 live pre-v4 pools across mainnet, preview and preprod — v1, v3 and Stableswaps — with `totalLp == current.quantityLP` in every single case, no exception.**

| network | pre-v4 pools sampled | `totalLp == quantityLP` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| mainnet | 139 | 139/139 |
| preview | 69 | 69/69 |
| preprod | 14 | 14/14 |

So one uniform mapping is correct. A version-aware branch would have two arms that provably agree for every pre-v4 pool — untestable, and an invitation to drift.

## The change

- `totalLp` is selected on all **seven** query paths and read by all **four** mappers.
- **No fallback to `current.quantityLP`.** The field is `BigInteger!` (NON_NULL) on all three gateways, and a fallback would silently reintroduce this exact bug on any path that later lost the selection.
- `IPoolData.liquidity.lpTotal` now documents what it means and why it is uniform across versions.
- `QueryProviderSundaeSwapLegacy` is **deliberately unchanged**: it queries the stats API, whose schema has no `totalLp` field at all, and which serves pre-v4 pools only — where the circulating supply is the right denominator.

## Verification

Checked before selecting, since a field one network lacks fails the whole query: mainnet, preview and preprod all resolve `totalLp` as `BigInteger!`.

Live through the real provider on all three networks:

```
preview  v4 stableswap  lpTotal = 20980352866116849   (circulating: 20980202970303189)
preprod  4 v4 pools     all positive, all matching the API's totalLp
mainnet  5 pre-v4 pools all resolve unchanged
```

Tests assert the **selection** on every query path, not just the mapping — the failure mode here is silence: the fetch succeeds and the number is quietly wrong. The fixture's `totalLp` is deliberately above its `quantityLP`, so a regression that reaches for the circulating figure produces a visibly different number rather than passing by coincidence. There is also a test pinning the pre-v4 case, where the two are equal.

313 core tests pass (3 skip, 0 fail), 180 math tests pass, lint 0 errors.

author: benhall-7
body:
Extension packages spawn their codec worker from a `blob:` URL. When a page's CSP forbids that (e.g. `worker-src 'self'`), the worker never loads, so no command ever gets a response and the whole conversion hangs forever with no error.

We're running Mediabunny in a Chrome extension on third-party pages whose CSP we don't control, so right now we just abandon the media conversion if it doesn't respond, but it would be better to catch it outright.

In #195 it was noted that CSP errors can't be caught because the `Worker` constructor doesn't throw. That's true, but the worker still fires an `error` event, which we can listen for.

## Changes

- `aac-encoder`, `flac-encoder`, `mp3-encoder`, `ac3`, `dts`: on worker `error`, reject all pending commands and fail any later ones immediately. The core already does this for its own workers in `media-source.ts` and `media-sink.ts`.
- `ac3`/`dts`: the shared worker's failure persists, since codec contexts live in its memory, and is cleared when the worker is terminated and replaced.
- `ac3`/`dts`: `close()` catches its fire-and-forget command so closing after a failure doesn't spit out an unhandled rejection.

## Tests

`test/browser/worker-csp.test.ts` injects a `worker-src 'self'` CSP and checks that each of the five encoders rejects. If you run it without the fix, all five time out, and with it they fail within milliseconds.
